row.basis: Moses asks to see divine glory
row.note: The commentary's Moses asks his Lord to show Himself at the appointed meeting (Q 7:143); here Moses asks YHWH to show him divine glory, making the mountain encounter a direct scene for comparison.

The commentary stresses that Moses is told he will not see God and then falls when the mountain is shattered; Exodus says no human can see God's face and live, framing the same sight-limit with a different outcome.

After shielding Moses, God lets him see the divine back while withholding the face; the Qur'anic scene in the commentary instead leaves Moses stunned before the flattened mountain, a distinct account of bounded sight.

The commentary contrasts Israel's demand to see God openly (Q 2:55) and the thunderbolt with Sinai's survivors saying they heard God speak from fire and lived; the different sensory demand changes the encounter.
Sarah laughs inwardly at the promise of a child; the commentary says the hidden thing may remain concealed even from its bearer, so this scene gives that claim a concrete human instance.
YHWH asks Abraham why Sarah laughed and repeats her unspoken thought; this exemplifies the commentary's claim that what stays inside a person is still known by God.

Hannah's lips move but her voice is not heard, and Eli mistakes her for drunk; this is the exact human-side contrast between audible prayer and inward speech developed around cehr and hidden recitation.

Samuel sees Eliab's appearance, while YHWH looks at the heart; the verse supplies a concrete limit to human visible judgment beside the commentary's claim that hidden and manifest are equal to God's knowledge.
Solomon asks God to hear each worshipper's prayer and answer because God alone knows human hearts; this joins hidden inward knowledge to the prayer setting emphasized in the commentary.

The Aramean king's secret plans reach Israel through Elisha, even though the king asks who is reporting his private words; this narrates the commentary's point that concealed speech is not concealed from God.

row.basis: eyes opened to the hidden host
row.note: Elisha's servant cannot see the fiery army surrounding them until his eyes are opened; the scene gives a concrete human limit to seeing what is present, alongside the commentary's open/hidden contrast.
God says He searches the heart and tests the inward parts; this is a direct biblical counterpart to the commentary's hidden thing that may have no humanly visible sign but remains known to God.

In the mining poem, a miner dams streams and brings hidden things to light; this is a concrete analogue to the commentary's secondary sense of drawing a concealed thing from under earth, while its context distinguishes human extraction from divine wisdom.
The poem says God looks to earth's ends and sees all beneath the heavens; that scope grounds the commentary's claim that no hidden thing needs a human sign to enter God's knowledge.

row.basis: no darkness for wrongdoers to hide in
row.note: Job says there is no darkness or deep shadow where evildoers can conceal themselves; the verse makes the commentary's hidden-versus-visible knowledge claim spatial and judicial.
The psalm says God understands the speaker's thought from afar; this directly supports the commentary's move from high-voiced words to what remains unspoken in the chest.

row.basis: word known before it is spoken
row.note: The psalm says the Lord knows a word before it is on the tongue; this closely matches the commentary's inward reading that has not yet become audible speech.

row.basis: darkness is not dark to God
row.note: The psalm says night is as bright as day to God; this gives a direct image for the commentary's paired hidden and manifest, including the limits of human sight at night.

The psalm asks whether God would not discover the injustice, since He knows the heart's secrets; this is a close counterpart to the commentary's claim that hidden things remain within divine knowledge.
Jeremiah asks whether anyone can hide in secret places beyond God's sight, since He fills heaven and earth; this gives a direct spatial formulation of the commentary's open/hidden pair.
Zion fears she has been forgotten, but God says even a mother might forget and He will not; this directly places human memory's failure beside the divine fidelity that frames 87:6–7.

row.basis: God remembers His covenant and word
row.note: The psalm says God remembers His covenant and command for a thousand generations; this directly joins divine memory to enduring revelation, as the commentary does for the promise to recite without forgetting.
Daniel's hymn says God reveals deep, hidden things, knows what is in darkness, and has light with Him; this gathers the commentary's concealment, disclosure, and light images in one claim.

row.basis: the sinner thinks darkness hides him
row.note: The sinner asks who can see him and trusts the dark and walls; the next verse overturns that confidence, matching the commentary's contrast between what a person thinks concealed and God's knowledge.
Sirach says God's eyes are brighter than the sun and inspect human paths and hidden places; this closely joins the commentary's sun-glare and secret-knowledge images.
Sirach says the Most High searches the abyss and the human heart and knows what can be known; this gives the commentary's inward hiddenness a Jewish wisdom-text counterpart.
Sirach says no thought escapes God and nothing is hidden from Him; this is a compact parallel to the commentary's unspoken or forgotten matter remaining within divine knowledge.

row.basis: witness of heart and hearer of tongue
row.note: Wisdom calls God witness of inmost feelings, overseer of the heart, and hearer of the tongue; it explicitly joins the inner and spoken domains paired in 87:7.
Wisdom says a jealous ear hears all things and no grumbling goes unheard; this gives the commentary's high and low speech distinction a divine-hearing counterpart.
Wisdom warns that no secret utterance is without consequence; this is especially close to the commentary's claim that an unvoiced or hidden word remains known.

row.basis: Hannah's silent prayer as a prayer rule
row.note: The rabbis derive prayer rules from Hannah's moving lips and unheard voice, including that prayer is inward and not raised aloud; this interprets the same scene used by the commentary's loud/quiet reading.
Jesus tells the disciple to pray in a closed room, while the Father sees in secret; this directly joins the commentary's inward, inaudible prayer to divine awareness.
Jesus says the Father knows what people need before they ask; this is a close counterpart to the psalmic and Qur'anic claim that God knows speech and thought before they are voiced.
Jesus says what was whispered in private rooms will be proclaimed from rooftops; this ties the commentary's quiet/high speech pair to a specific disclosure saying.

Jesus promises that the Spirit will teach and remind the disciples of what he said; this is a Christian counterpart to the surrounding promise that prophetic recitation and memory are given, not owned by the messenger.

row.basis: Jesus knows what is in people
row.note: The narrator says Jesus knew what was in each person; this gives the commentary's claim about God's knowledge of inward contents a distinct Christian narrative counterpart.

Peter identifies Ananias's hidden plan to lie about the money; the episode makes an inward intention known in the community, matching the commentary's claim that concealment does not remove a matter from divine knowledge.

row.basis: darkness and heart-counsels brought to light
row.note: Paul says the Lord will expose what is hidden in darkness and disclose the purposes of hearts; this closely matches both halves of the commentary's open/hidden knowledge claim.
Hebrews says no creature is hidden from God's sight and all are exposed before Him; this is a direct statement of the commentary's central reason for the exception clause.

Paul describes God as dwelling in inaccessible light, whom no human has seen or can see; this adds a Christian formulation of the visual limit that the commentary develops through sun-glare and Moses.

row.basis: God does not forget faithful work
row.note: Hebrews says God is not unjust so as to forget the community's work and love; this supplies a Christian counterpart to the commentary's contrast between human forgetting and divine remembrance.

James corrects merchants' confident plans with “if the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that”; this is a close Christian counterpart to the commentary's Q 18:23–24 example of human plans resting on divine willing.

row.basis: Jesus' words do not pass away
row.note: In an eschatological warning, Jesus says heaven and earth will pass away but his words will not; this supplies a Christian permanence claim beside the commentary's discussion of God retaining or replacing revealed words.

row.basis: divine address in a thin quiet sound
row.note: Elijah encounters YHWH after wind, earthquake, and fire in a quiet, delicate sound; this gives the commentary's low-voice side a theophanic setting without making it equivalent to the ayah's claim.
Elijah's servant sees only a hand-sized cloud rising from the sea before the storm; this fits the commentary's faint sign at a cloud edge and its link between barely visible weather and rain.
The small cloud becomes a sky dark with clouds and heavy rain; this completes the specific hidden-sign-to-visible-rain sequence the commentary joins to the surah's pasture scene.

row.basis: dawn attack while the enemy is unaware
row.note: The commentary notes a secondary cehr usage for a surprise dawn raid; Saul's forces strike Ammon at the morning watch before the camp wakes, supplying that precise military image.
Jacob finds a well whose mouth is covered by a large stone; this gives a concrete biblical object for the commentary's well whose water is hidden beneath a covering.
The shepherds roll the stone away and water the flock; this matches the commentary's image of removing a covering so concealed well-water becomes available.
God sets the rainbow as a sign of the covenant; beside the commentary's claim that divine knowledge needs no visible marker, this gives a concrete biblical role for a sign.

row.basis: God sees the sign and remembers
row.note: The text says God will see the bow and remember the everlasting covenant; this differs from the commentary's account of knowledge needing no landmark, without requiring that Genesis portray God as forgetful.

The verse assigns hidden things to YHWH and revealed things to Israel and its children; unlike the commentary's claim that both are equally known to God, it marks a boundary between divine and human knowledge.

row.basis: humans must not add or subtract
row.note: Israel is forbidden to add to or subtract from the commandments; beside the commentary's claim that God may remove or replace revelation, this distinguishes divine authority over a word from human tampering.

The prophet contrasts withering grass and fading flowers with God's enduring word; this is a direct permanence counterpart to the commentary's assurance that the given recitation remains by divine will.

row.basis: words placed in the mouth will not depart
row.note: God promises that His Spirit and words put in the addressee's mouth will remain through descendants; this closely parallels the commentary's reading of recitation as a gift sustained by God.

Jehoiakim cuts the prophetic scroll and burns it, a human attempt to erase a revealed word; the commentary's account of divine removal and replacement makes this hostile destruction a useful contrast.

row.basis: the burned scroll is written again
row.note: God tells Jeremiah to take another scroll and rewrite the words; this gives a narrative counterpart to the commentary's discussion of revelation being removed or replaced under divine direction.
Moses says these words are to be upon Israel's heart; this concretely parallels the commentary's word held inwardly before it is voiced or remembered.
The word is said to be near, in mouth and heart; this brings the commentary's public recitation and inwardly held word together in one scriptural formulation.
The psalmist stores God's word in the heart; this is a direct image for the commentary's recitation remaining inwardly present even when not spoken.
Ezekiel eats the scroll and it becomes sweet in his mouth; this gives bodily form to the commentary's image of revelation taken into the prophet and held within.

row.basis: radiant face after speaking with God
row.note: Moses' face shines after speaking with YHWH; the scene gives a concrete biblical instance of divine encounter exceeding ordinary sight, beside the commentary's sun-glare and human visual limit.
Moses covers his face after delivering God's words; this joins the commentary's veil/visibility imagery to the spoken revelation Moses carries.

row.basis: worship and the glory of God's name
row.note: The psalm joins worship with giving glory to YHWH's name; this is a specific liturgical counterpart to the commentary's emphasis that Allah's name appears at the hinge and is praised in al-Fatiha.

The proverb uses milk-churning to illustrate a result forced by an action; the commentary's churn image likewise describes butter gathering out of milk, though it uses the process for emergence rather than strife.
After describing human mining for hidden ore, Job says God understands wisdom's way and knows its place; this contrasts human excavation with the commentary's divine knowledge of what remains hidden.

The Mishnah says there is a seeing eye, a hearing ear, and deeds written in a book; this concretely combines sight, sound, and record beside the commentary's claim that speech and hidden things are known.

The Talmud interprets Moses' permitted sight of God's back as the knot of God's tefillin; this gives a Jewish reading of the bounded vision in Exodus that complicates the commentary's account of Moses' request.

row.basis: what is hidden will be disclosed
row.note: Jesus says concealed things are destined to be revealed; this resonates with the commentary's secondary reading of the hidden as only a step from being brought out, while the Qur'anic verse itself stresses knowledge rather than disclosure.
James quotes merchants planning where they will travel and trade tomorrow; his next verse conditions action on the Lord's will, closely matching the commentary's Q 18:23–24 example.

Jesus says the day and hour are known only to the Father; this parallels the commentary's distinction between a messenger's limited knowledge and God's knowledge, while giving that distinction a different Christian formulation.

Paul says the Spirit searches everything, even God's depths; this offers a Christian account of access to hidden knowledge, though its focus is the Spirit's knowledge of God rather than human secrets.

Paul contrasts present dim sight and partial knowledge with future face-to-face knowledge; this adds a Christian account of human limits beside the commentary's contrast between God's full knowledge and human perception.
John says no one has ever seen God, while the Son makes Him known; this gives a Christian version of the sight-limit in the commentary's Moses scene, with revelation mediated through the Son.
Paul recalls Moses veiling his face so Israel would not gaze at the fading glory; this directly extends the commentary's visibility and covering images from a different reading of Moses.

row.basis: veil over readers of the old covenant
row.note: Paul interprets Moses' veil as a veil over minds when the old covenant is read, removed in Christ; this Christian rereading turns a physical covering into an interpretive barrier beside the commentary's hidden/revealed reading.
Paul calls the community a letter written by the Spirit on hearts rather than stone; this gives a Christian image for the commentary's recited word held inwardly.
Paul applies Deuteronomy's near word to the message of faith; this repeats the commentary's meeting of audible recitation and inwardly held speech in a Christian setting.
At the Transfiguration Jesus' face shines like the sun; this gives the commentary's image of brightness overwhelming human sight a distinct Christian mountain theophany to compare.
Moses appears with Elijah and speaks with Jesus; beside the commentary's focus on Moses seeking a vision at Sinai, this is a distinct Christian scene of Moses within a mountain revelation.
A cloud overshadows the disciples and a voice speaks from it; this adds a specific spoken revelation from a hidden cloud beside the commentary's open/hidden voice pair.
After the cloud's voice, the disciples fall facedown in fear; this parallels the commentary's account of Moses collapsing before the mountain manifestation, while the scene's outcome differs.
Jesus says the water he gives becomes a spring within the recipient; this is a specific Christian counterpart to the commentary's image of remembered revelation as water held inside a well.

row.basis: all things exist by God's will
row.note: The heavenly hymn says all things were created and exist by God's will; this gives a conceptual counterpart to the commentary's Arabic wordplay joining willing and thinghood, without claiming a cognate.

row.basis: human addition to prophecy warned against
row.note: Revelation warns against adding to the prophetic book; beside the commentary's account of God replacing verses, it distinguishes divine action from a reader's unauthorized alteration.

row.basis: human removal from prophecy warned against
row.note: Revelation warns against taking words from the prophetic book; this sharpens the commentary's distinction between God's authority over revelation and human control of its wording.

Jesus contrasts eternal punishment with eternal life; beside the commentary's reading of the Qur'anic exception as not cutting off an unending gift, this supplies a different formulation of final duration.

Hebrews says the promised new covenant makes the first obsolete and near disappearance; this is a Christian example of revelation's covenantal form changing, adjacent to the commentary's discussion of replacing verses.

row.ref: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Moses II.162–164
row.note: Gregory reads Moses' ascent into cloud and darkness as a deeper knowledge of the God who cannot be seen; this Christian interpretation changes the commentary's sight-limit scene into a path of knowing through unseeing.

row.basis: Jacob says he saw God and lived
row.note: Jacob names Peniel because he saw God face to face and his life was spared, a specific counterpoint to the commentary's Moses scene; the opponent's identity and the meaning of seeing God remain ambiguous in Genesis.

Moses recalls Israel standing before a mountain of fire, cloud, and thick darkness; this is a specific Sinai setting beside the commentary's account of Moses and Israel confronting the limits of divine sight.
At Horeb Israel hears God's voice from the fire but sees no form; this makes the commentary's pairing of recited sound and restricted vision an explicit feature of the same revelation scene.
Moses repeats that Israel saw no form and therefore must not make an image; beside Q 7:143, this gives a distinct scriptural consequence of a theophany without visible form.

While the people stand at a distance, Moses approaches the thick darkness where God is; this makes hiddenness the setting of direct encounter, complementing the commentary's open/hidden knowledge pair.
The people hide their counsel in darkness and ask who sees them; this is a direct prophetic example of the concealment the commentary says cannot remove anything from divine knowledge.
The psalm asks whether the one who planted the ear cannot hear and the one who formed the eye cannot see; this joins the commentary's audible and visual forms of cehr to their divine source.
The psalm says YHWH knows human thoughts; this gives a concise counterpart to the commentary's hidden contents remaining known even when not voiced.
Hannah's song says YHWH is a God of knowledge who weighs actions; after her silent prayer, this connects the commentary's prayer scene to divine knowledge and judgment.

row.basis: elders think God does not see
row.note: In Ezekiel's vision, elders worship in hidden rooms and say YHWH does not see them; the scene supplies a concrete false belief that the commentary's open/hidden knowledge claim overturns.

row.basis: God knows what comes to mind
row.note: YHWH says He knows what comes into the people's minds; this is a direct counterpart to the commentary's unspoken contents of the heart being within divine knowledge.
Ecclesiastes says God brings every work, including every hidden thing, into judgment; this extends the commentary's claim that hidden matters remain known to a concrete judgment scene.
A book of remembrance is written before YHWH for those who fear His name; this joins the commentary's linked themes of divine memory, recorded words, and the name invoked in worship.

row.basis: no one can hide from God
row.note: Sirach challenges the person who thinks they can be hidden from the Lord among the crowd; this gives a distinct wisdom-text setting for the commentary's claim that no concealed thing escapes divine awareness.

row.basis: secret almsgiving seen by the Father
row.note: Jesus says the Father sees charitable giving done in secret; this extends the commentary's open/hidden pair from prayer and recitation to a specific concealed ethical action.
Jesus says what is covered will be revealed and what is hidden will be known; this is a direct continuation of the commentary's claim that hiddenness does not mean disappearance from knowledge.
Jesus says people will answer for every careless word; this applies the commentary's claim about God's knowledge of speech to words that speakers might treat as unimportant.

row.basis: Spirit supplies the persecuted speaker's words
row.note: Jesus tells disciples not to prepare their defense because the Holy Spirit will give them what to say; this is a Christian counterpart to the commentary's insistence that prophetic speech is given rather than owned.

Peter says prophecy did not arise from human will, but people spoke from God as carried by the Holy Spirit; this directly parallels the commentary's claim that the messenger does not possess the source of recitation.

row.basis: God judges human secrets through Christ
row.note: Paul says God judges people's secrets through Christ; this gives a Christian judgment formulation for the hidden contents that the commentary says God knows.
Christ says He searches minds and hearts and repays each according to deeds; this joins inward knowledge to judgment, as the commentary's account of hidden matters does.
John sees the dead judged from opened books according to their deeds; this gives an apocalyptic record-and-disclosure counterpart to the commentary's claim that God counts what people forget.

At the temple dedication Solomon says YHWH has chosen to dwell in thick darkness; this supplies a distinct biblical way to pair God's presence with concealment beside the commentary's manifest/hidden knowledge.

Isaiah calls YHWH the God who hides Himself and Israel's Savior; this adds a biblical theme of divine hiddenness to the commentary's distinction between God being hidden from human sight and knowing what is hidden.
God gives Moses His name as a memorial through generations; this complements the commentary's claim that the divine name at the ayah's hinge belongs to worship and remembrance, not impersonal fate.

row.basis: Israel's confession of the one YHWH
row.note: The Shema names YHWH as Israel's one God; beside the commentary's emphasis on Allah's name at the exception clause, this gives a central Jewish liturgical confession to read alongside al-Fatiha.

row.basis: love YHWH with the whole heart
row.note: The Shema immediately commands love of YHWH with all heart, soul, and strength; this concretely joins the divine name to worshipful devotion as the commentary does.

row.basis: stones as a sign for future questions
row.note: Joshua sets stones as a sign so children will ask what they mean; this gives a concrete human use of visible markers beside the commentary's claim that God's knowledge does not need a sign.
The stones are to be a memorial for Israel; this shows a community using a visible sign to preserve memory, contrasting with the commentary's divine knowledge that needs no landmark.

The Mishnah says all is foreseen while freedom is granted; this is a specific Jewish formulation of the tension between divine knowing and human willing that the commentary resolves through God's will.

row.basis: all is in Heaven's hands except awe of Heaven
row.note: The Talmud places everything in Heaven's hands except reverence of Heaven; this gives a rabbinic boundary to divine sovereignty beside the commentary's claim that human plans and memory remain dependent on God's will.

row.basis: God works both willing and doing
row.note: Paul says God is at work in believers both to will and to act; this closely parallels the commentary's claim that even human willing depends on God.

row.basis: Peter remembers after Jesus looks at him
row.note: After the rooster, Jesus looks at Peter and Peter remembers Jesus' prediction; this gives a narrative instance of a forgotten word returning when the commentary says remembering follows forgetting.
